cloze.text: Furcation involvement is the loss of {{c1::interradicular}} bone on {{c2::multirooted}} teeth.
The {{c1::Naber's probe}} (furcation probe) is used to assess the presence and extent of a furcation.
Radiographs are used to check furcation defects but are not completely reliable, because {{c1::overlapping tooth structures}} can mask the bone loss.
On a radiograph, a radiolucency between the roots indicates a furcation defect of Class {{c1::II}} and above.
Tooth-loss risk by furcation class: Class I {{c1::8%}}; Class II {{c2::22%}}; Class III {{c3::47%}}.
Mandibular molars are usually {{c1::bifurcated}} ({{c2::mesial and distal}} roots), with potential furcation involvement on the {{c3::facial and lingual}} aspects.
Maxillary molars are usually {{c1::trifurcated}} ({{c2::mesiobuccal, distobuccal and palatal}} roots), with potential furcation involvement on the {{c3::facial, mesial and distal}} aspects.
Maxillary {{c1::first premolars}} can have bifurcated roots ({{c2::buccal and palatal}}), with potential furcation involvement on the {{c3::mesial and distal}} aspects.
Glickman {{c1::Class I}} furcation: the curvature of the concavity can be detected with the probe tip, but the probe cannot enter the space; {{c2::no}} radiolucency on radiographs.
Glickman {{c1::Class II}} furcation: the probe penetrates the furcation more than {{c2::1 mm}} but does not pass completely through to the other side; slight radiolucency may be visible.
Glickman {{c1::Class III}} furcation: the probe passes {{c2::completely through}} the furcation; a radiolucency is usually visible on radiographs.
Glickman {{c1::Class IV}} furcation: the entrance to the furca is {{c2::clinically visible}} and the probe passes completely through; a larger radiolucency is visible.
{{c1::Bitewing}} radiographs are used for interproximal caries detection.
{{c1::Vertical}} bitewings are preferred over horizontal bitewings to assess bone level when bone destruction occurs.
{{c1::Periapical}} radiographs are used for periodontal evaluation (bone-loss pattern and level, abscess) and for root abnormalities such as {{c2::dilaceration and resorption}}.
{{c1::Occlusal}} radiographs are useful to locate {{c2::sialoliths}} and for patients who have difficulty opening the jaw; commonly used for pediatric patients.
{{c1::Panoramic}} radiographs are useful to assess third molars, eruption patterns and TMJ problems; also indicated for patients who have difficulty opening the jaw or are {{c2::edentulous}}.
{{c1::Smoking}} is the most significant systemic risk factor for periodontal disease; the primary cause of periodontal disease is {{c2::plaque biofilm}}.
cloze.extra: Don't confuse risk factor (smoking) with cause (biofilm). The exam records smoking as cigarettes per day (1 pack = 20).

cloze.text: Systemic conditions such as {{c1::diabetes}} also influence the periodontal disease process and healing time.
Other important periodontal risk factors: gender ({{c1::men}}), {{c2::older}} age, insufficient nutritional intake, and {{c3::parafunctional}} habits.
Oral cancer: {{c1::alcohol}} consumption in conjunction with {{c2::smoking}} greatly increases the risk of oral cancer.

Caries: the {{c1::consumption pattern}} of cariogenic food increases caries risk; other important risk factors include low socioeconomic status, lack of home care and insufficient {{c2::fluoride}} exposure.

Recall radiographs, child (primary dentition): low caries risk = posterior bitewings every {{c1::12–24}} months; increased caries risk = every {{c2::6–12}} months — both only if proximal contacts cannot be visualized.
cloze.extra: Schedule adapted from Darby's Dental Hygiene (5th ed.), radiographic guidelines & CAMBRA.

cloze.text: Recall radiographs, adolescent (mixed or permanent dentition): low caries risk = posterior bitewings every {{c1::18–36}} months if contacts cannot be visualized; increased caries risk = every {{c2::6–12}} months.
cloze.extra: Schedule adapted from Darby's Dental Hygiene (5th ed.), radiographic guidelines & CAMBRA.

cloze.text: Recall radiographs, adult (dentate or partially edentulous): low caries risk = posterior bitewings every {{c1::24–36}} months; increased caries risk = every {{c2::6–18}} months.
cloze.extra: Schedule adapted from Darby's Dental Hygiene (5th ed.), radiographic guidelines & CAMBRA.

cloze.text: New patient, child (primary or mixed dentition): {{c1::periapicals and/or bitewings}}, taken only if proximal surfaces cannot be visualized.
cloze.extra: Schedule adapted from Darby's Dental Hygiene (5th ed.), radiographic guidelines & CAMBRA.

cloze.text: New patient, adolescent or adult: {{c1::bitewings + panoramic}} OR {{c2::bitewings + selected periapicals}}.
cloze.extra: Schedule adapted from Darby's Dental Hygiene (5th ed.), radiographic guidelines & CAMBRA.

cloze.text: Have the patient {{c1::demonstrate}} how they use the brush and floss, to evaluate how they can improve.
Patients should brush a minimum of {{c1::2}} times per day for {{c2::2}} minutes.
Recommend {{c1::soft}} bristles with {{c2::rounded}} nylon filaments.
The {{c1::diameter}} of the filament determines the hardness of a toothbrush.
{{c1::Nylon}} filaments are more resistant to bacteria and dry more easily than natural bristles.
Advise patients to develop a brushing {{c1::sequence}}.
Bass method: bristles into the sulcus at 45°; {{c1::small vibratory circular}} motions. It is the {{c2::most accepted}} method because it cleans the sulcus — excellent for plaque below the gumline.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Are we STILL ON for dinner?" → STILLman = ON the gums. CHART AWAY → Charter's is AWAY from the gingiva. See the O in fOnes → O = circular motion.

cloze.text: Stillman method: bristles on the gingiva angled apically at 45° (not into the sulcus); {{c1::small vibratory}} motions; used for {{c2::gingival stimulation}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Are we STILL ON for dinner?" → STILLman = ON the gums. CHART AWAY → Charter's is AWAY from the gingiva. See the O in fOnes → O = circular motion.

cloze.text: Charter's method: bristles directed toward occlusal; {{c1::back-and-forth vibratory}} strokes; bristles do not enter the sulcus; used for {{c2::orthodontics, prostheses and post-surgical areas}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Are we STILL ON for dinner?" → STILLman = ON the gums. CHART AWAY → Charter's is AWAY from the gingiva. See the O in fOnes → O = circular motion.

cloze.text: Fones method: bristles perpendicular to the teeth; {{c1::large circular}} motions; used for {{c2::children and physically impaired}} patients; {{c3::not recommended for adults}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: "Are we STILL ON for dinner?" → STILLman = ON the gums. CHART AWAY → Charter's is AWAY from the gingiva. See the O in fOnes → O = circular motion.

cloze.text: The Modified Bass and Modified Stillman's methods combine the original technique with a {{c1::rolling sweep}}.
Power toothbrushes were originally developed for patients with {{c1::disabilities}}.
Power toothbrushes can also be recommended for patients with appliances, restorations, low {{c1::motivation}}, periodontal disease, poor biofilm control and lack of manual {{c2::dexterity}}.
Both manual and power toothbrushes are dependent on {{c1::technique}} — emphasize correct use.
The {{c1::tongue}} is the largest surface of the oral cavity and retains a lot of bacteria.
Clean the tongue with a tongue cleaner or a toothbrush; emphasize tongue cleaning to patients with {{c1::black hairy tongue}} or {{c2::halitosis}}.
Studies show the type of floss (waxed or unwaxed) does {{c1::not}} make a difference in plaque removal; the patient can choose by preference.
{{c1::Waxed}} floss can be more comfortable for tight contacts.
Tufted dental floss is useful for an implant, fixed bridge, {{c1::distal surface of the last tooth}} in the arch, proximal surfaces of widely spaced teeth, and type {{c2::II or III}} embrasures.
A {{c1::floss handle}} is best for patients with larger hands or who lack manual dexterity.
A floss threader allows floss to access under an {{c1::abutment, pontic, bridge}}, orthodontic appliance and implant.
Super floss is ideal for {{c1::orthodontics, bridges and implants}}.
A {{c1::wooden wedge}} cleans type II or III embrasures and furcations.
The interdental (interproximal) brush cleans type II or III embrasures, exposed furcations and exposed {{c1::root concavities}}.

The {{c1::end-tuft brush}} cleans type III embrasures, the distal surface of the last tooth, the lingual surface of mandibular teeth (or difficult-to-reach areas), exposed furcations and orthodontic appliances.
A {{c1::toothpick}} (in holder) cleans type II or III embrasures, the gingival margin and furcations.
A water flosser flushes areas of the oral cavity with {{c1::pulsating}} water, but cannot clean the {{c2::contact area}} of adjacent teeth.

Power flossers (air and water types) are useful for orthodontic appliances, restorations and implants, and for patients who lack dexterity or motivation; they cannot clean the contact area, so use them as an {{c1::adjunct}}.
cloze.extra: Did you know: a 2019 systematic review (Journal of Dental Hygiene) found water flossers effective at reducing gingival inflammation, but insufficient evidence that they are superior to floss for plaque removal.

cloze.text: Oral irrigation helps reduce {{c1::bleeding and gingival inflammation}}; adjunct therapeutic agents such as {{c2::antimicrobials}} can be added to the water.
Per the manufacturer, the subgingival irrigator tip delivers water that penetrates up to {{c1::90%}} in pockets of {{c2::6 mm}} or less.
The subgingival irrigator tip is used to deliver a {{c1::medicament}} into difficult-to-access areas and should be used {{c2::after}} the standard tip.
Xerostomia increases the risk of caries, especially {{c1::root surface}} caries, and contributes to {{c2::halitosis}}.
For xerostomia, recommend saliva {{c1::substitutes}} and saliva {{c2::stimulants}} to maintain moisture and comfort.
For xerostomia, encourage frequent {{c1::sips of water}} and sucking on {{c2::ice chips}} throughout the day.
For xerostomia, recommend sugar-free gum, sugar-free candies and {{c1::xylitol}} products to stimulate salivary flow.
Xerostomia patients should avoid mouthrinses containing {{c1::alcohol}}, which can further dry oral tissues.
For xerostomia, provide {{c1::fluoride}} therapy (e.g., varnish, Rx toothpaste) to prevent and manage caries.
Recommend {{c1::Biotène}} or similar products to relieve the symptoms of dry mouth.
Most halitosis is caused by {{c1::volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs)}}, produced when {{c2::anaerobic}} bacteria break down {{c3::proteins}} in the mouth.
Halitosis bacteria thrive in low-{{c1::oxygen}} environments, including periodontal pockets, the {{c2::posterior tongue}} and around the tonsils.
{{c1::Tongue coating}} is the most common cause of halitosis in healthy individuals.
For halitosis, recommend daily tongue cleaning with a {{c1::tongue scraper or toothbrush}} to reduce odor-producing bacteria and debris.
For halitosis, use alcohol-free mouthrinses containing {{c1::chlorine dioxide}}, {{c2::zinc compounds}} or {{c3::sodium bicarbonate}} to neutralize odors and reduce VSC levels.
Halitosis may be caused by non-oral factors such as {{c1::GERD}}, stomach ulcers ({{c2::H. pylori}}), tonsillitis or sinus infections.
Halitosis may also be associated with periodontal disease, carious lesions, poor oral hygiene or ill-fitting {{c1::appliances}}.
"How do you feel about your home care routine?" is an example of an {{c1::open-ended question}} (MI).
"So it sounds like flossing feels like too much right now." is an example of {{c1::reflective listening}} (MI).
"You're brushing twice a day — that's a great start!" is an example of an {{c1::affirmation}} (MI).
In MI, {{c1::summarizing}} means restating the patient's concerns, progress and goals.
In MI, {{c1::Elicit–Provide–Elicit}} means asking permission before giving advice, then checking for understanding.

OHI for an orthodontic patient: tools = {{c1::end-tuft brush, proxy brush, floss threaders, fluoride rinse}}; advice = emphasize cleaning around brackets and use MI to discuss effort and appearance goals.

OHI for an implant patient: tools = {{c1::nylon-coated}} interdental brush, super floss, non-abrasive toothpaste; advice = avoid {{c2::metal-core}} brushes and discuss {{c3::peri-implantitis}} prevention.

OHI for a gingivitis patient: tools = soft-bristled brush, floss, antimicrobial rinse (e.g., {{c1::chlorhexidine}}); advice = reinforce technique and set short-term goals for {{c2::bleeding reduction}}.

OHI for a periodontitis patient: tools = power brush, interproximal brush, rubber tip, floss, fluoride toothpaste; advice = teach access to deep pockets and emphasize {{c1::3}}-month re-care and inflammation control.
OHI for a child: tools = small brush head, flavored fluoride paste, {{c1::disclosing tablets}}, supervision; advice = involve the {{c2::parent}} and teach technique in fun, age-appropriate ways.
OHI for an elderly / arthritic patient: tools = electric toothbrush, floss holder, {{c1::enlarged handles}}; advice = support limited dexterity and address {{c2::dry mouth}} if present.
OHI for a xerostomia patient (table): fluoride toothpaste/rinse, Biotène products, sugar-free xylitol gum; avoid {{c1::alcohol-based}} rinses and reinforce {{c2::caries}} prevention.
OHI for a bridge or pontic: tools = {{c1::tufted floss, floss threader, end-tuft brush}}; advice = show technique for cleaning under pontics and practice with a {{c2::mirror}}.

OHI for a tobacco user: tools = power brush, antimicrobial rinse, {{c1::stain-removing}} toothpaste; advice = link OHI with stain control and cancer-risk reduction, using a {{c2::nonjudgmental}} tone.
{{c1::Inactive}} ingredients — coloring, flavoring, preservative, thickener (water and glycerin), whitening agent — do not have a therapeutic effect.
In dentifrices, the thickener ingredients are {{c1::water and glycerin}}.
{{c1::Systemic}} delivery = a drug given as a tablet or capsule that is absorbed into the bloodstream (e.g., {{c2::Periostat}}).
{{c1::Local}} delivery = the agent is delivered to the desired area (e.g., dentifrices, mouthrinses).
{{c1::Antimicrobial}} agents reduce or inhibit biofilm activity (e.g., cetylpyridinium chloride, chlorhexidine, sanguinarine, phenolic compounds, triclosan).
{{c1::Oxygenating}} agents (hydrogen peroxide) debride and release oxygen.
{{c1::Astringents}} shrink tissue (e.g., citric acid, zinc chloride).
{{c1::Desensitizing}} agents reduce dentinal hypersensitivity (e.g., stannous fluoride, potassium nitrate).
{{c1::Anodynes}} (analgesics) alleviate pain (e.g., benzocaine, lidocaine).
{{c1::Buffering}} agents reduce acidity, dissolve mucinous films and relieve soft-tissue pain.
{{c1::Deodorizing}} agents (sodium bicarbonate) and {{c2::oxidizing}} agents (chlorine dioxide) neutralize odors and eliminate VSCs.
Fluorides decrease dental {{c1::caries}} risk; whitening agents such as {{c2::hydrogen peroxide}} reduce extrinsic stains.
Mouthrinses are recommended as {{c1::adjuncts to}}, not replacements for, mechanical plaque biofilm control.
Mouthrinses are effective on {{c1::supragingival}} biofilm only, unless delivered subgingivally with {{c2::irrigators}}.
Chlorhexidine (CHX) rinse active ingredient: {{c1::0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate}}.
Of the common mouthrinses (CHX, essential oils, CPC, sanguinarine, oxygenating, fluoride), only {{c1::chlorhexidine}} requires a prescription.
{{c1::Essential oil}} rinses contain thymol, menthol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate.
The active ingredient of quaternary ammonium rinses is {{c1::cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC)}}.
Sanguinarine is extracted from the {{c1::bloodroot}} plant.
cloze.extra: Did you know: a natural plant-based alkaloid (Sanguinaria canadensis), once used in rinses and dentifrices for antimicrobial properties; now rarely used due to limited clinical evidence and concerns over safety and effectiveness.

cloze.text: Oxygenating rinse active ingredients: {{c1::hydrogen peroxide}} and {{c2::carbamide peroxide}}.
The active ingredient of fluoride rinses is {{c1::sodium fluoride (NaF)}}.
Chlorhexidine has {{c1::high}} substantivity, lasting {{c2::8–10}} hours.
CHX rinse contains about {{c1::11%}} alcohol (alcohol-free versions available).
CHX main uses: {{c1::gingivitis}}, periodontitis, {{c2::candidiasis}} and post-op care.
CHX is for {{c1::short-term}} use only; rinse {{c2::15 mL}} for {{c3::30 sec}} BID; also used as a rinse before dental procedures.
CHX side effects: {{c1::staining}}, increased {{c2::calculus}}, taste alteration and dry mucosa.
Avoid CHX in {{c1::alcohol-sensitive}} individuals (unless using an alcohol-free version). Brands: Peridex®, PerioGard®.
Essential oil rinses have {{c1::low}} substantivity and about {{c2::21–26%}} alcohol (some alcohol-free options).
Essential oil rinse main uses: gingivitis and as a {{c1::preprocedural}} rinse; use as an adjunct, not a replacement for brushing.
Essential oil rinse side effects: {{c1::burning}}, dryness, altered taste.
Essential oil rinses are contraindicated for {{c1::alcohol-dependent}} patients or those with {{c2::xerostomia}}.
CPC (quaternary ammonium) rinses have {{c1::very low}} substantivity and up to {{c2::20%}} alcohol.
CPC rinse main uses: mild gingivitis, {{c1::fresh breath}}; often added to OTC rinses for branding, not well supported by evidence.
CPC side effect: mild {{c1::staining}} possible; limited benefit for {{c2::periodontal disease}}.
Sanguinarine rinse has {{c1::minimal}} substantivity and about 15% alcohol; it must be used with {{c2::Viadent}} toothpaste to be effective (gingivitis).
cloze.extra: Book: no well-documented side effects, outdated use, not widely used, limited evidence.

cloze.text: Oxygenating rinses have very low substantivity and variable alcohol; main use = short-term {{c1::wound cleaning}} and minor irritations.
Oxygenating rinses are not for long-term daily use; weak against biofilm. Long-term use can cause tissue damage, ulceration and {{c1::black hairy tongue}}.
cloze.extra: Book's table: avoid with open wounds and long-term use. Brands: Amosan®, hydrogen peroxide.

cloze.text: Fluoride rinses have {{c1::moderate}} substantivity and are {{c2::alcohol-free}}; main use = remineralization and caries prevention.
Fluoride rinses are great for {{c1::high caries risk}}, ortho or exposed roots; minimal side effects if used properly; use daily for at-risk patients.
Sodium fluoride toothpaste: OTC = {{c1::0.24%}} NaF / 1100 ppm; Rx = {{c2::1.1%}} NaF / 5000 ppm.
Sodium fluoride toothpaste helps {{c1::remineralize}} enamel and prevent demineralization; essential for {{c2::high caries risk}} patients.
{{c1::Stannous fluoride}} toothpaste is used for caries prevention, anti-gingivitis and anti-plaque.
Stannous fluoride releases {{c1::tin}} ions with an antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory effect.
Stannous fluoride may cause {{c1::extrinsic brown staining}}, especially with poor plaque control.
{{c1::Potassium nitrate}} toothpaste is used for dentin hypersensitivity relief.
Potassium nitrate blocks nerve transmission by {{c1::depolarizing}} sensory nerve endings.

basic.back: A combination of bitewings and periapicals that provides images of all teeth present in the oral cavity
Thin piece of straight plastic with a loop on one end
Pre-cut floss with a stiff end, a sponge section and regular floss
Tapered rubber tip that massages the gingiva and removes plaque at the gingival margin
The area where the water initially contacts the surface
The pocket/sulcus area where the solution penetrates
A patient-centered communication style that helps patients explore and resolve ambivalence about behavior change
The component that produces the therapeutic effect (e.g., sodium fluoride for caries protection)
The ability of an agent to bind to tissues and be retained/released slowly over time, with a continued effect

basic.front: Why does potassium nitrate reduce dentinal hypersensitivity — and why only while it is being used?
basic.back: It diffuses into the dentinal tubules and depolarizes the nerve endings, keeping the nerve in a constant low-level excited state so it responds less to external stimuli (cold, touch). The numbing-like effect lasts only while the product is in use.

mcq.question: While probing #30, the Naber's probe passes from the buccal furcation completely through to the lingual. The furca entrance is covered by gingiva and not clinically visible. Which Glickman class is this?
mcq.explanation: Class III = the probe passes completely through the furcation. Class IV also passes through, but its furca entrance is clinically visible; Class II penetrates >1 mm without passing through.

mcq.question: On which aspects should the hygienist check for furcation involvement on a maxillary first molar?
options: D. Facial, lingual, mesial and distal
mcq.explanation: Maxillary molars are trifurcated (MB, DB, palatal roots), so furcations open on the facial, mesial and distal. Facial and lingual is the pattern for bifurcated mandibular molars.

mcq.question: A patient has generalized moderate horizontal bone loss. Which bitewing orientation best shows the bone level?
mcq.explanation: Vertical bitewings are preferred over horizontal bitewings for assessing bone level when destruction occurs, because the taller image captures more of the crestal bone. Horizontal bitewings are for interproximal caries.

mcq.question: A 45-year-old dentate recall patient has several new carious lesions (increased caries risk). How often should posterior bitewings be taken?
mcq.explanation: Adults at increased caries risk: posterior bitewings every 6–18 months. 6–12 months is the interval for children and adolescents at increased risk; 24–36 months is for low-risk adults.

mcq.question: A hygienist places the bristles partly on the attached gingiva, angled apically at 45°, and uses small vibratory motions without entering the sulcus. Which method is this?
mcq.explanation: Stillman = bristles ON the gingiva, angled apically, for gingival stimulation. Bass also uses 45°, but the bristles go INTO the sulcus.

mcq.question: Which toothbrushing method is most appropriate for a patient with fixed orthodontic appliances?
mcq.explanation: Charter's method directs bristles toward occlusal with back-and-forth vibratory strokes, which suits orthodontics, prostheses and post-surgical areas. Fones is for children and is not recommended for adults.

mcq.question: A patient has gingival recession with an exposed root concavity and an exposed furcation on #19. Which aid is most appropriate?
mcq.explanation: The interdental brush cleans type II/III embrasures, exposed furcations and exposed root concavities. Floss cannot adapt into a concavity; a floss threader only carries floss under fixed appliances.

mcq.question: Which statement about oral irrigation is correct?
options: A. The standard tip is inserted at 45° into the pocket
B. Water flossers clean the contact area of adjacent teeth
C. The subgingival tip is used after the standard tip to deliver medicaments
D. The impact zone is the pocket area the solution penetrates
mcq.answer: C. The subgingival tip is used after the standard tip to deliver medicaments
mcq.explanation: The subgingival rubber tip (45° into the pocket) delivers medicaments and follows the standard tip. The standard tip sits at 90°; irrigators cannot clean contacts; the pocket area penetrated is the flushing zone, not the impact zone.

mcq.question: A healthy 30-year-old with good periodontal health complains of bad breath. What is the most likely cause?
mcq.explanation: Tongue coating is the most common cause of halitosis in healthy individuals — anaerobes on the posterior tongue produce VSCs. GERD and sinus infections are non-oral causes and less common.

mcq.question: The hygienist asks, "Would it be OK if I shared a tip about flossing?", explains the tip, then asks, "How might that fit into your evening?" Which MI technique is this?
mcq.explanation: Elicit–Provide–Elicit = ask permission, give the advice, then check understanding/response. Reflective listening restates what the patient said; it does not give advice.

mcq.question: A patient with two implants asks which interdental brush to use. What should the hygienist recommend?
options: A. A standard metal-core interproximal brush
D. A floss threader with waxed floss only
mcq.explanation: For implants the book recommends a nylon-coated interdental brush (plus super floss and non-abrasive paste) and says to avoid metal-core brushes.

mcq.question: A patient using a prescribed rinse after periodontal surgery returns with brown extrinsic stain and increased supragingival calculus. Which rinse is most likely responsible?
mcq.explanation: Chlorhexidine's side effects are staining, increased calculus, taste alteration and dry mucosa; it is the only one of these that needs a prescription. Essential oils cause burning and dryness, not calculus.

mcq.question: A patient with xerostomia and high caries risk asks for a daily mouthrinse. Which is the best choice?
options: A. Essential oil rinse with 26% alcohol
mcq.explanation: Fluoride rinses are alcohol-free, remineralize, and are meant for daily use in at-risk patients. Essential oil rinses are contraindicated in xerostomia (alcohol dries tissue); CHX is short-term only; peroxide is not for long-term daily use.

mcq.question: A patient with gingivitis reports new brown extrinsic stain since switching toothpastes. Which active ingredient is most likely responsible?
mcq.explanation: Stannous fluoride (anti-gingivitis, anti-plaque via tin ions) may cause extrinsic brown staining, especially with poor plaque control. Sodium fluoride and potassium nitrate are not linked to staining in the book.
